posts.title: You paid to generate the enquiry

copy.default:
You paid to generate the enquiry.

Then you let the prospect disappear after one follow-up.

That is one of the strangest things businesses do.

Money goes into:

Ads.

Content.

The website.

Social media.

Referral offers.

Then someone actually raises their hand...

…and the system for converting that interest is basically:

“Send them something and hope they reply.”

Three days later:

“Maybe we need more leads.”

Maybe.

But first I want to know what happened to the people who already wanted something.

Who enquired?

Who booked?

Who disappeared?

Who cancelled?

Who was followed up once?

Who should have been followed up again?

Growth is not only about putting more people into the top.

Sometimes it is about stopping valuable people quietly falling out of the bottom.

If I walked into an appointment-led business on Monday morning, I would not start by asking about followers.

I would ask for five lists:

1. People who enquired but never booked.
2. People who cancelled.
3. People who no-showed.
4. Clients who should probably have returned by now.
5. Good past clients nobody has contacted properly in months.

That is where I would start looking for growth.

Not because everybody on those lists can be recovered.

They cannot.

But because those people already know the business.

Some already wanted the service.

Some already trusted it enough to buy.

And businesses can spend huge amounts of energy acquiring strangers while barely touching the demand they already created.

Before asking:

“How do we get another 100 leads?”

I would ask:

“What happened to the last 100?”

That answer can change the entire growth plan.

Here is a piece of maths more businesses should do.

Illustrative example, not a client result:

Say 20 past clients should normally return during a month.

Average visit value: £80.

But only 12 come back.

The missing eight represent £640 of potential booking value.

That does not mean £640 is automatically recoverable.

Some will have moved.

Some changed provider.

Some no longer need the service.

Some simply will not return.

But if nobody knows why they disappeared and there is no structured return journey, the business has no idea whether it lost:

£0.

£160.

£320.

Or the entire £640 opportunity.

That uncertainty is the interesting part.

You cannot recover every customer.

But you can stop treating every unexplained disappearance as inevitable.

An empty appointment slot expires.

That is what makes service-business capacity interesting.

A product sitting on a shelf can often still be sold tomorrow.

Tuesday at 2:30pm cannot.

Once Tuesday at 2:30pm passes empty, that capacity is gone.

Which means a quiet diary is not just a marketing problem.

It can be a timing problem.

A client intended to rebook but forgot.

Someone cancelled and nobody filled the slot.

An enquiry went cold two days earlier.

A past client would happily have returned but was never prompted.

None of those require the business to suddenly become famous.

They require a better connection between existing demand and available capacity.

I think that is why Revenue Recovery is such an interesting space.

Sometimes the growth opportunity has an expiry time.

A no-show is not only a lost appointment.

It can become a lost customer.

The obvious response is:

Send a reminder before the appointment.

Good.

But what happens after they miss it?

Does the relationship just stop?

Does someone remember to message them later?

Does the booking system create a clear return path?

Does the client know how easily they can rearrange?

The interesting part is that the original appointment already proved intent.

They booked.

That makes a no-show different from a cold lead.

I would rather build a sensible recovery path around existing intent than immediately spend money trying to manufacture brand-new intent.

Prevent the no-show where possible.

Recover the relationship when prevention fails.

posts.title: Memory is not the booking system

copy.default:
“I'll book later” is not a booking system.

Neither is:

“I'll remember to message her.”

“I think he normally comes every six weeks.”

“She said she would get back to us.”

“We haven't seen them for ages.”

These sound harmless because each one involves a person who might return.

But “might” is exactly the problem.

Human memory becomes the CRM.

Staff availability becomes the automation.

Good intentions become the follow-up process.

And eventually someone gets forgotten.

The best systems are rarely about pestering customers more.

They are about making sure the right person receives the right reminder at a sensible moment without the whole thing depending on somebody remembering.

Less chasing.

Fewer forgotten opportunities.

Better timing.

posts.title: Where is existing demand being lost?

copy.default:
Revenue Recovery starts with a different question.

Most growth conversations begin with:

“How do we generate more demand?”

We prefer:

“Where is existing demand already being lost?”

That can include:

Enquiries that never become bookings.

Cancellations that are never recovered.

No-shows with no structured return path.

Clients who lapse without a rebooking prompt.

Dormant customers nobody reactivates.

Automations that exist but no longer work as intended.

Acquisition still matters.

But increasing the amount entering a system without understanding what leaks out can make the underlying problem more expensive.

The first job is not automatically more traffic.

It is visibility.

Find the leak.

Understand the mechanism.

Then decide whether the opportunity is worth recovering.

posts.title: An enquiry is evidence of intent

copy.default:
An enquiry is not just a name in an inbox.

It is evidence of intent.

Someone:

Found the business.

Considered the service.

Took an action.

Then something happened.

They booked.

They delayed.

They chose somebody else.

They became distracted.

They received a weak response.

They were never followed up.

Or nobody knows.

That final category matters.

If an appointment-led business cannot distinguish between:

“not interested”

and

“never properly followed up”

then it cannot accurately diagnose its acquisition performance.

Before increasing lead generation, map what happens after the enquiry.

A stronger acquisition engine feeding a weak follow-up system creates a bigger leak.

COMMON:

“Just checking if you still want to book?”

BETTER:

A follow-up that gives the customer a useful reason to move.

Context.

Clarity.

An easy next action.

Good follow-up does not mean sending more messages for the sake of it.

It means removing the reason the decision stalled.

Maybe the customer needed to understand availability.

Maybe the treatment or service was unclear.

Maybe they were not ready that day.

Maybe the next step felt unnecessarily difficult.

The goal is not persistence at any cost.

The goal is to make an appropriate buying decision easier.

That is a fundamentally different approach to “chasing leads”.

A quiet week should trigger more than a last-minute discount.

Discounting is one lever.

It is not the only one.

Before reducing price, an appointment-led business can ask:

Who is due to return?

Who recently cancelled?

Who enquired but never booked?

Who used to buy this service regularly?

Who expressed interest in something relevant?

Who can lawfully and appropriately be contacted?

The business may already have several pools of existing demand.

The commercial challenge is connecting the right pool to the right opening without turning the database into a broadcast list.

Quiet capacity is more useful when it becomes a recovery signal rather than a panic signal.

posts.title: Rebooking should not rely on reception memory

copy.default:
The easiest rebooking system is not:

“Remember to ask at reception.”

That can work.

Until the team is busy.

Someone is covering a shift.

The customer leaves quickly.

Or the conversation simply gets missed.

A stronger system does not remove the human moment.

It protects it.

If the customer does not rebook immediately, there is another appropriate route.

Timing reflects the normal service cycle.

Messages recognise whether someone has already booked.

People who should not receive the reminder are excluded.

Results can actually be measured.

The objective is not “more automation”.

It is fewer good clients relying entirely on memory to come back.

posts.title: Prevention and recovery are different jobs

copy.default:
Prevention and recovery are different jobs.

A reminder can reduce the chance of a missed appointment.

But once the appointment is missed, the customer is in a different state.

They may need:

A simple rescheduling route.

A different message.

A human follow-up.

A pause before another reminder.

Or no further contact.

A system designed only to prevent no-shows has no answer once prevention fails.

That is why lifecycle design matters.

Customer journeys do not always follow the ideal path.

The recovery route should exist before it is needed.

Retention gets easier when you stop organising customers only by demographics.

A more useful question is:

What state is the customer currently in?

For an appointment-led business, states might include:

Enquired.

Booked.

Upcoming appointment.

Attended.

Due to rebook.

Overdue.

Cancelled.

No-show.

Dormant.

Reactivated.

Each state contains a different job.

The person who enquired but never booked does not need the same message as the loyal client who is simply overdue.

The no-show does not need the same journey as the two-year dormant customer.

Lifecycle marketing becomes more useful when the state determines the treatment.

Not the marketing calendar.

A simple lifecycle can be written as:

Interest → Booking → Attendance → Return → Repeat

Then ask one question between every stage:

What can break here?

Interest → Booking
Slow response. Confusing next step. Weak follow-up.

Booking → Attendance
Poor reminders. Friction. Changed circumstances.

Attendance → Return
No rebooking path. Wrong timing. No follow-up.

Return → Repeat
Irrelevant communication. Service-cycle mismatch. Relationship decay.

The purpose of a leakage map is not to assume every drop-off is recoverable.

It is to make the unknown visible.

Once the breakpoints are visible, you can decide which ones are economically worth fixing.

Sending more messages is often the least interesting lifecycle optimisation.

Timing can matter far more.

A reminder three weeks too early can be irrelevant.

The same reminder at the natural decision window can feel useful.

A win-back message sent immediately after somebody's normal return date may be premature.

Six months later may be meaningless.

A cancellation recovery message can be valuable while intent is still fresh.

Three months later it is a different conversation.

Lifecycle systems should ask:

What happened?

When did it happen?

What normally happens next?

When does intervention become useful?

Volume is easy to see.

Timing is where a lot of the intelligence lives.

There is no such segment as “everyone who hasn't purchased recently”.

At least, not if you want the message to mean anything.

A better breakdown might be:

Recently overdue regulars.

One-time customers.

Former high-frequency clients.

Recent cancellations.

Previously engaged enquiries.

Long-term dormant customers.

People already booked again.

People who should not be contacted.

Notice what happened there.

The segmentation moved from:

“Who can we send to?”

towards:

“Who is in a customer state where this message makes sense?”

That is a much safer and more commercially useful question.

A rebooking reminder needs a model of expected return.

Even a simple one.

Suppose Customer A normally returns every four weeks.

Customer B returns every twelve.

Sending both the same “time to book again” message after six weeks creates two different mistakes.

For A, it may be late.

For B, it may be annoying.

You do not always need predictive AI.

You need sensible timing logic.

Service type.

Previous behaviour.

Normal interval.

Recent booking status.

Exclusions.

Then test.

A basic model that reflects reality can outperform sophisticated automation built on the wrong assumption.

A no-show should change the customer's state.

That sounds obvious.

Operationally, it often is not.

The customer may remain inside the same generic reminder or promotional logic as everybody else.

A better journey recognises:

Appointment scheduled.

Reminder sent.

Appointment missed.

Existing future booking check.

Appropriate recovery contact.

Rescheduled or unresolved.

Exit.

That state change matters because the customer context changed.

Lifecycle automation is not merely a sequence of messages.

It is a set of rules for responding to behaviour.
